{{Short description|Theorem of mathematical logic}}
'''Robinson's joint consistency theorem''' is an important theorem of [[mathematical logic]]. It is related to [[Craig interpolation]] and [[Beth definability]].

The classical formulation of Robinson's joint [[consistency]] theorem is as follows:

Let <math>T_1</math> and <math>T_2</math> be [[First-order logic|first-order]] [[Theory (mathematical logic)|theories]]. If <math>T_1</math> and <math>T_2</math> are [[consistent]] and the intersection <math>T_1 \cap T_2</math> is [[Complete theory|complete]] (in the common language of <math>T_1</math> and <math>T_2</math>), then the union <math>T_1 \cup T_2</math> is consistent. A theory <math>T</math> is called [[Complete theory|complete]] if it decides every formula, meaning that for every [[Sentence (mathematical logic)|sentence]] <math>\varphi,</math> the theory contains the sentence or its negation but not both (that is, either <math>T \vdash \varphi</math> or <math>T \vdash \neg \varphi</math>).

Since the completeness assumption is quite hard to fulfill, there is a variant of the theorem:

Let <math>T_1</math> and <math>T_2</math> be [[First-order logic|first-order]] theories. If <math>T_1</math> and <math>T_2</math> are consistent and if there is no formula <math>\varphi</math> in the common language of <math>T_1</math> and <math>T_2</math> such that <math>T_1 \vdash \varphi</math> and <math>T_2 \vdash \neg \varphi,</math> then the union <math>T_1\cup T_2</math> is consistent.

== Proof ==
For a first-order language <math>L</math> and a set <math>S</math>, let <math>L_S</math> denote the language obtained from <math>L</math> by adding 0-ary operations bijectively corresponding to the set <math>S</math>. For a first-order language <math>L</math>, an <math>L</math>-structure <math>M</math> and a subset <math>S\subseteq M</math>, let <math>M_S</math> denote the <math>L_S</math>-structure obtained from <math>M</math> by interpreting each 0-ary operation <math>s\in S</math> as <math>s</math> itself. For a first-order language <math>L</math>, its expansion <math>L'</math> and an <math>L'</math>-structure <math>M</math>, let <math>M\restriction L</math> denote the reduct of <math>M</math> in <math>L</math>.

Let <math>L</math> be a first-order language and <math>L_1</math> and <math>L_2</math> its expansions such that <math>L_1\cap L_2=L</math>. Let <math>T_1</math> be a consistent theory in <math>L_1</math> and <math>T_2</math> a consistent theory in <math>L_2</math>. Suppose that <math>T_1\cap T_2</math> is a complete theory in <math>L</math>. We shall show that <math>T_1\cup T_2</math> is a consistent theory.

Using the [[compactness theorem]], it is not hard to show that, for every <math>L_1</math>-structure <math>M</math> and an <math>L_2</math>-structure <math>N</math>, if <math>M\restriction L</math> is [[elementarily equivalent]] to <math>N\restriction L</math>, then the theory
:<math>\operatorname{Th}(M_M)\cup\operatorname{Th}((N\restriction L)_N)</math>
is [[satisfiable theory|satisfiable]].

For an <math>L_1</math>-structure <math>M</math> and an <math>L_2</math>-structure <math>N</math>, if <math>M\restriction L</math> is elementarily equivalent to <math>N\restriction L</math>, then for some <math>L_1</math>-structure <math>M'</math>, there exist an <math>L_1</math>-[[elementary embedding]] <math>M\hookrightarrow M'</math> and an <math>L</math>-elementary embedding <math>N\restriction L\hookrightarrow M'\restriction L</math>. Indeed, take an <math>(L_1)_{M,N}</math>-model
:<math>M''\models\operatorname{Th}(M_M)\cup\operatorname{Th}((N\restriction L)_N)</math>
and put <math>M'=M''\restriction L_1</math>.

Now take a model <math>M_0\models T_1</math> and a model <math>N_0\models T_2</math>. Since <math>T_1\cap T_2</math> is an <math>L</math>-complete theory, we have <math>T_1\cap T_2=\operatorname{Th}(M_0\restriction L)=\operatorname{Th}(N_0\restriction L)</math>. Therefore, there exist an <math>L_2</math>-structure <math>N_1</math>, an <math>L_2</math>-elementary embedding <math>N_0\hookrightarrow N_1</math> and an <math>L</math>-elementary embedding <math>M_0\restriction L\hookrightarrow N_1\restriction L</math>. Again, since <math>(L_1)_{M_0}\cap(L_2)_{M_0}=L_{M_0}</math> and <math>(M_0\restriction L)_{M_0}</math> is elementarily equivalent to <math>(N_1\restriction L)_{M_0}</math>, there exist an <math>(L_1)_{M_0}</math>-structure <math>(M_1)_{M_0}</math>, <math>(L_1)_{M_0}</math>-elementary embedding <math>(M_0)_{M_0}\hookrightarrow(M_1)_{M_0}</math> and an <math>L_{M_0}</math>-elementary embedding <math>(N_1\restriction L)_{M_0}\hookrightarrow(M_1\restriction L)_{M_0}</math>. In particular, there exist an <math>L_2</math>-structure <math>M_1</math>, an <math>L_1</math>-elementary embedding <math>M_0\hookrightarrow M_1</math> and an <math>L</math>-elementary embedding <math>N_1\restriction L\hookrightarrow M_1\restriction L</math>.

By induction, there exist <math>L_1</math>-structures <math>M_0,M_1,\dots</math>, <math>L_2</math>-structures <math>N_0,N_1,\dots</math> and elementary embeddings
:<math>M_i\hookrightarrow M_{i+1}</math>
:<math>N_i\hookrightarrow N_{i+1}</math>
:<math>M_i\restriction L\hookrightarrow N_{i+1}\restriction L</math>
:<math>N_{i+1}\restriction L\hookrightarrow M_{i+1}\restriction L</math>
which make the following diagram commute.
:<math>\begin{matrix}
M_0 & \to & M_1 & \to & M_2 & \to & \cdots \\
& \searrow & \uparrow & \searrow & \uparrow & \searrow & \cdots \\
N_0 & \to & N_1 & \to & N_2 & \to & \cdots
\end{matrix}</math>
(In the above diagram, the horizontal arrows are elementary embeddings in <math>L_1</math> or <math>L_2</math>, and the vertical and diagonal arrows are elementary embeddings in <math>L</math>.) Finally, the [[colimit]] of the above diagram is easily seen to be a model of <math>T_1\cup T_2</math>.
